title: Believe: A Bible Study for New Believers and Seekers
subtitle: A five-session study on what Christians actually believe, and why it is both reasonable and life-giving.
summary:
This study is for new believers taking their first steps, for seekers circling the faith with real questions, and for small groups willing to slow down and ask what the gospel is before anyone is asked to sign on to it. Drawn from my book Believe, its five sessions ask whether there is a God at all and what kind; who Jesus claimed to be and why the claim can't be sidestepped; whether he actually rose from the tomb; what faith and doubt really are; and what it costs, and gives, to follow him. A busy volunteer can lead it with no preparation. Every question comes with a note for the leader, and every session ends in prayer rather than in winning an argument.

The study doesn't treat doubt as the enemy or seekers as projects to be closed, and the leader shouldn't either. Faith isn't the absence of questions, and a faith that has never been tested isn't strong, only untested. Some objections to Christianity are weak and fall apart on their own. Others are serious and have been asked by the church's best minds for two thousand years, and those deserve a real answer, not a slogan. The study tries to hold both.
audience: New believers, seekers, small groups, and adult Sunday school

sessions.title: Is There Anyone There
sessions.aim: To ask the first question fairly, whether there is a God at all and what kind, refusing both the believer who treats the question as settled before it's asked and the skeptic who treats unbelief as an obvious default that needs no defense.
sessions.summary:
Many people would like to believe but can't make themselves; it feels like wishing on a star. So we start where everyone actually starts: is there anyone there? One answer says belief is obvious, that the world plainly declares a maker. It's right that the existence of something rather than nothing begs for an explanation. Another says unbelief is the grown-up default, that science has filled the gaps God used to fill and faith is a comfort for people who can't bear a meaningless world. It's right that some belief is exactly that.

Neither gets to win cheaply. The world doesn't prove God the way a theorem proves a conclusion. But unbelief isn't a neutral, cost-free starting point either; the atheist also has to explain why there's something rather than nothing, and why the universe is a place where minds can ask the question. The evidence points without forcing. "The heavens declare the glory of God" (Psalm 19:1), and a person can follow that pointing without pretending to a certainty no one has.

keyScripture.why: "The heavens declare the glory of God, and the sky above proclaims his handiwork" (Psalm 19:1). The psalmist doesn't argue God into existence. He points, treating the world itself as a witness that speaks without words to anyone willing to look.

discussion.q: Before tonight, what did you privately believe about God? That he's obviously there, obviously not, or that you've never let yourself decide?
discussion.behind: Bring the default into the open before defining anything. Most people carry an unexamined verdict, often inherited, and have rarely said it aloud. Don't settle it yet. Go first if the room is slow.

discussion.q: What's the difference between evidence that proves and evidence that points? Which kind do most of your deepest convictions rest on?
discussion.behind: Many seekers think faith requires certainty and reject it for lack of one. Help them see that most real convictions, about people we trust or things we're sure are right, rest on a weight of evidence, the way a jury's verdict does, not on a mathematical proof.

discussion.q: Is unbelief a neutral starting point, or does it have questions of its own to answer? Do you want to push back on that?
discussion.behind: This is the hinge, and it shouldn't become a debate to win. Keep it on the recognition that belief and unbelief both carry a burden. No one stands on neutral ground. That levels the table, so the seeker isn't the only one asked to defend a view.

discussion.q: Some people say faith is a crutch for those who can't bear a meaningless world. What's true in that, and what does it leave out?
discussion.behind: Some belief really is wishful, and the seeker should hear the church admit it. But the charge cuts both ways: unbelief can be a wish too, the wish to have no one to answer to. Don't let the room leave thinking only believers have motives.

discussion.q: Read Psalm 19:1-4. How does the psalmist make his case? What would it look like to listen to the world the way he does?
discussion.behind: He doesn't argue; he points. "Day to day pours out speech" (Psalm 19:2). Let the room notice that Scripture's first move toward God is attention, not a proof. End on that, not on a verdict.

objections.objection: Science has explained what religion used to explain. We don't need God for lightning or disease or the origin of species, so God is just the shrinking gap in our knowledge, and one day the gap will close.
objections.response: Part of this is right. Science has explained mechanisms earlier generations attributed directly to God, and a god who only hides in the gaps of our ignorance will keep losing ground. That god is worth giving up. But science explains how the universe works, the chain of cause and effect inside it. It doesn't explain why there's a universe at all, or why it's ordered in a way minds can understand. Those aren't gaps in the science. They're questions science has to assume an answer to before it can begin. The God Christians mean isn't a competing mechanism inside the universe. He's the reason there's a universe with mechanisms in it.

objections.objection: If you only believe because you were born into a Christian family in a Christian country, your faith is an accident of geography. Born somewhere else, you'd believe something else.
objections.response: Much of that is true. A lot of belief is inherited and never examined, and a faith that has only ever been the local default deserves some suspicion. But the argument proves too much. It applies to everything you believe, including unbelief. A skeptic raised among skeptics would believe something else if born elsewhere too. Where you started tells you nothing about whether a thing is true, only where you began looking. The real question isn't where your belief came from. It's whether, examined as an adult, it turns out to be true.

sessions.quietRoomQuestion: If God is real, and not a distant clockmaker but a Father who wants to be known, what in you most resists wanting that to be true?
sessions.practice: This week, do what the psalmist did. Once a day, go outside and look at something you didn't make and can't fully explain: the sky, a tree, your own hand. Stay with it long enough to feel how strange it is that it exists at all. Then ask, not "Is this proof?" but "What is this pointing to?" Write down what comes up, including any resistance, and don't judge it.
sessions.closingPrayer: God, if you're there, and we're asking in earnest, you know that some of us have wanted you to be real and couldn't make ourselves believe, and some of us have wanted you not to be real and couldn't quite shake the sense that you are. Meet us in the wanting and the resisting. We're tired of inherited answers we never chose. Give us courage to look at the world and at ourselves without flinching, and if you're the one the heavens are declaring, help us begin to hear it. We come with our questions, not our conclusions. Amen.
reflection: What have I believed about God mainly because it was handed to me?
Do I demand a kind of proof for God that I don't demand for any other deep conviction I hold?
If there's no God, what would I have to account for, and have I ever tried?
sessions.teaching:
Many people who come to a study like this would like to believe but can't make themselves. The whole thing feels like wishing on a star, and they want to know how an honest person even begins. That's the right question, and this whole study is built to take it seriously, because one of the worst things the church can do to a seeker is rush him past the first question to get to the invitation. So we begin where everyone begins. Not with how to have faith, but with the question before it: is there anyone there at all?

Two answers want to silence each other, and I want to hear each at its strongest. The first says belief is obvious. It points to the sheer existence of things, the order of the cosmos, the beauty no struggle for survival required, and concludes with the psalmist that "the fool says in his heart, 'There is no God'" (Psalm 14:1). It isn't wrong to be struck by this. The universe didn't have to exist, and it does, and it's the kind of place where dust eventually wakes up and asks who made it.

The second answer says unbelief is the grown-up default. It points to the long retreat of God before advancing science, and to the way faith so often comforts exactly the people who most need comfort. It concludes that belief is a crutch, a wish dressed up as a fact. That isn't entirely wrong either. Some belief is exactly that. There are people whose god is mostly a hedge against the fear of dying, and a believer should admit it.

Now watch what happens when neither answer is allowed the whole field. The world doesn't prove God the way a theorem proves a conclusion. Anyone who says it's just obvious has never sat across from a thoughtful atheist who isn't a fool, and there are many. The evidence points; it doesn't force. A reasonable, intelligent person of good will can look at the same world and not be compelled, which means belief is a verdict reached on a weight of evidence, the way a jury reaches one.

But the other edge cuts just as deep. Unbelief isn't the neutral, cost-free default it often presents itself as. The atheist doesn't get to stand on empty ground and make the believer do all the explaining. He too has to account for why there's something rather than nothing, why the universe is ordered so that physics works at all, and why a meaningless accident of chemistry should produce minds that hunger for meaning and a sense of right and wrong that feels like more than preference. "I just lack a belief" sounds modest, but once you ask the deep questions, everyone has a view to defend. There's no view from nowhere.

I don't say this from a safe distance. I came to faith out of atheism. I've sat on the other side of this table and meant my objections. And I know that the word "Father," which the Bible uses for God, isn't an easy or sentimental word for everyone in this room. Some of you will need to hear it slowly.

Notice how Scripture itself handles the question, because it isn't what we expect. Psalm 19 doesn't offer a proof. "The heavens declare the glory of God, and the sky above proclaims his handiwork. Day to day pours out speech, and night to night reveals knowledge. There is no speech, nor are there words, whose voice is not heard" (Psalm 19:1-3). The psalmist points. He treats the world as a witness that speaks to anyone willing to stand still and listen, the way Jesus would later answer worry by saying, "Look at the birds of the air" (Matthew 6:26). Paul makes a similar claim: God's "invisible attributes, namely, his eternal power and divine nature, have been clearly perceived, ever since the creation of the world, in the things that have been made" (Romans 1:20). And he tells the philosophers in Athens that God made us "that they should seek God, and perhaps feel their way toward him and find him. Yet he is actually not far from each one of us" (Acts 17:27). Feeling your way is allowed.

The case for God isn't a closed file. But it's a real case, and the seeker doesn't have to wait for a certainty no one has. He only has to be willing to follow the pointing and see where it leads, which is what the next sessions ask.

scriptureStudy.note: "The heavens declare the glory of God, and the sky above proclaims his handiwork." Not a proof but a pointing. Belief begins with attention to what's already in front of us.

"His invisible attributes, namely, his eternal power and divine nature, have been clearly perceived... in the things that have been made." Paul claims creation makes God knowable in a basic way to everyone. The pointing is real, even if it doesn't force.
"That they should seek God, and perhaps feel their way toward him and find him. Yet he is actually not far from each one of us." Paul allows for groping in the dark, treating seeking as a real path.
"Whoever would draw near to God must believe that he exists and that he rewards those who seek him." Faith here isn't blind. It's the trust of someone who has begun to seek and expects to be met.
"The fool says in his heart, 'There is no God.'" Blunt, but notice the denial is located in the heart, not only the head. Unbelief can be a stance of the will as much as a conclusion of the mind.
"He has put eternity into man's heart." The Preacher names a hunger the world can't satisfy, which an accidental universe would have no reason to produce.
"The true light, which gives light to everyone, was coming into the world." The seeker isn't starting from nothing, only learning to name a light that was already there.

sessions.goingDeeper:
The arguments for and against God are old, and the church has done its best thinking under pressure. The cosmological argument, that a universe that didn't have to exist needs a cause that does, was refined by Thomas Aquinas in the thirteenth century as one of his "five ways." He called them ways, paths along which the mind moves toward God, not demonstrations that force belief. In the eighteenth century David Hume pressed hard on the argument from design and on miracles, and in the early twenty-first century writers such as Richard Dawkins and Christopher Hitchens revived his objections with real force. Read them fairly.

Then read the serious replies: Alvin Plantinga on why belief in God can be rational without being proven, and C. S. Lewis and later Timothy Keller on moral obligation, beauty, and longing as evidence that points beyond the material. A group might hold this session's discipline: refuse the lazy believer who thinks the question is too easy and the lazy skeptic who thinks it's too settled. The existence of God is the kind of large question, like the meaning of a life or the reality of love, that evidence bears on without ever closing like a math problem.
sessions.caseStudy:
Suppose a graduate student comes to your group sure he's the only unbeliever in the room and braced for a fight. He grew up hearing that real Christians don't have questions, and he has a list: suffering, the silence of God, miracles in a scientific age. He expects to be argued at. Instead you ask him to state his strongest objection, and then you agree that it's a good one and that the church has often answered it badly.

Notice what that does. It isn't a clever proof that moves him. It's discovering that his question is welcome and that no one needs him to lose so they can win. Ask your room: when have you experienced the difference between being argued at and being taken seriously, and which one ever changed your mind about anything that mattered?

sessions.title: Who Did Jesus Think He Was
sessions.aim: To take seriously what Jesus actually claimed, rather than the polite modern version of him, refusing both the believer who skips past the scandal of those claims and the skeptic who reduces him to a nice teacher.
sessions.summary:
Everyone has a Jesus. The skeptic has a wise moral teacher, the activist a revolutionary, the comfortable a gentle friend who agrees with them. The question is whether any of these is the man in the documents. The Jesus of the Gospels forgives sins, accepts worship, says "before Abraham was, I am" (John 8:58), and tells people that what they do with him decides what becomes of them.

Many people want to keep his ethics and drop his claims. The appeal is real; the Sermon on the Mount is magnificent. But C. S. Lewis argued that a man who said what Jesus said doesn't leave us the option of calling him merely a great moral teacher. Either the claims are true, or he was lying, or he was badly deluded. Some skeptics add a fourth possibility, that the claims are legend added later, and that question belongs to the next session. The scandal isn't that Jesus asks to be admired. It's that he asks for everything.

keyScripture.why: "And when Jesus saw their faith, he said to the paralytic, 'Son, your sins are forgiven.' Now some of the scribes were sitting there, questioning in their hearts, 'Why does this man speak like that? He is blaspheming! Who can forgive sins but God alone?'" (Mark 2:5-7). The scribes understood the claim better than many modern admirers do.

discussion.q: Before tonight, who was Jesus to you? A teacher, a myth, a friend, someone you admired from a distance? Where did that picture come from?
discussion.behind: Almost everyone carries a version of Jesus assembled from culture rather than from reading the Gospels. Bring it into the open so the rest of the session has somewhere to go.

discussion.q: Read Mark 2:1-12. Why are the scribes so upset? What did they understand about what Jesus had just done?
discussion.behind: Forgiving sins committed against God was something only God could do. The scribes weren't fools. Help the room feel the small shock of seeing that Jesus' own opponents took his claims more seriously than many admirers do.

discussion.q: What's appealing about keeping Jesus' ethics and dropping his larger claims? Why does Lewis think that can't be done?
discussion.behind: Hold both halves. The wish is reasonable and the ethics are admirable. But the man teaching the ethics also made claims that, if false, would discredit his judgment about everything else. Present the argument without swinging it like a club.

discussion.q: Some skeptics say the claims were added by the church later. How would you go about finding out?
discussion.behind: Take this seriously; it's the strongest version of the objection. Note that it moves the question onto history, which is where the next session goes. Don't force a verdict tonight.

discussion.q: Where do you keep Jesus at the level of admiration so you don't have to deal with him as Lord?
discussion.behind: Admiration is safe and costs nothing, and most of us prefer it. Go first, gently.

objections.objection: Jesus was a great moral teacher, maybe the greatest, and that's enough. Keep "love your enemies" and care for the poor, and leave the supernatural claims. You don't have to think he was God to learn from him.
objections.response: The appeal is real. The teaching is luminous, and the world would be better for following it. But the same man who taught us to love our enemies also said that he and the Father are one, that he could forgive sins, that he would judge the living and the dead, and that what a person does with him settles their eternity. If those claims are false, he wasn't a wise and humble teacher. Either he was lying, which ruins the moral authority you wanted to keep, or he was deeply deluded about who he was, which undermines his judgment about everything else. That's the heart of Lewis's argument in Mere Christianity: you can reject him or you can worship him, but the one thing you can't honestly do is pat him on the head as a fine human teacher while ignoring the claims that, if untrue, would make him nothing of the kind.

objections.objection: He never said any of that. The divine claims were added by the church decades later to build a religion. The real Jesus was a Jewish teacher, and the God talk is legend.
objections.response: This is the most serious form of the objection, and it deserves more than a wave. Legends do grow, and what Jesus actually said is a real historical question, not an insult to the faith. But legend usually needs time, and the earliest sources are early. Paul passes on a creed about Jesus' death, burial, and resurrection (1 Corinthians 15:3-5) that many scholars date to within a few years of the crucifixion, and the Gospels were written within the lifetime of people who had known him. The fair path isn't to assume the claims were added or to assume they weren't, but to ask what the evidence supports, which is the question of the next session. Hold it open, and don't let anyone close it cheaply in either direction.

sessions.quietRoomQuestion: If Jesus is who he said he was, and not just a teacher you can admire from a safe distance, what would change tomorrow morning? Is that the real reason you keep him at arm's length?
sessions.practice: This week, read the Gospel of Mark straight through, slowly, as if you'd never heard of it. It takes about an hour. Don't study it; just meet the man in it. Mark every place he says or does something a merely human teacher would have no business saying or doing. At the end, ask yourself which of the possibilities you're standing in front of, and which one you're avoiding.
sessions.closingPrayer: Jesus, we've made you small enough to admire and safe enough to ignore, a teacher we can quote and a friend who never asks for anything. Forgive us for the Jesus we invented to avoid the one who is real. Give us courage to read the Gospels and meet you as you are: the one who forgives sins, accepts worship, and asks for everything. Not all of us believe yet, and we won't pretend we do. But we're willing to look. Show us who you are, and give us the honesty to deal with the answer. Amen.
reflection: Which Jesus have I been carrying, and how much of him came from the Gospels?
Which possibility am I standing in front of, and which am I working hardest to avoid?
Where do I keep Jesus at the level of admiration because surrender would cost too much?
sessions.teaching:
Everyone has a Jesus. The skeptic keeps a wise moral teacher, a first-century rabbi with unusually good ethics. The activist keeps a revolutionary who sided with the poor against the powerful. The comfortable keep a gentle friend who happens to agree with all their opinions. These versions share the same problem: none of them is the man in the documents. The first task is to set down the Jesus we inherited and pick up the one who actually speaks in the Gospels, because that one is far stranger and far more demanding.

Read the texts without soft focus and watch what he says. A paralyzed man is lowered through a roof, and Jesus says, "Son, your sins are forgiven" (Mark 2:5). The scribes in the room understand exactly what he has done. "Why does this man speak like that? He is blaspheming! Who can forgive sins but God alone?" (Mark 2:7). They're right that only God can forgive sins committed against God. Jesus doesn't correct their theology. He heals the man so they'll know "that the Son of Man has authority on earth to forgive sins" (Mark 2:10).

It isn't an isolated moment. He accepts worship that prophets and angels in the Bible refuse. He says, "Truly, truly, I say to you, before Abraham was, I am" (John 8:58), taking onto his own lips the name God gave Moses at the burning bush, and his hearers pick up stones. He says, "I and the Father are one" (John 10:30), and when he asks why they want to stone him, they answer, "because you, being a man, make yourself God" (John 10:33). He taught "as one who had authority, and not as their scribes" (Matthew 7:29). On trial for his life, asked whether he's "the Christ, the Son of the Blessed," he answers, "I am, and you will see the Son of Man seated at the right hand of Power" (Mark 14:61-62). These aren't marginal sayings. They run all through the material.

So take the modern instinct at its strongest, because many of us lean on it. Keep the ethics and drop the metaphysics. Keep "love your enemies" and "turn the other cheek," which are magnificent, and quietly let go of the supernatural claims, which are embarrassing. You don't have to think Socrates was divine to learn from him, so why Jesus? The appeal is real. A world that lived the Sermon on the Mount would be better by any measure.

But C. S. Lewis, in Mere Christianity, named why the move breaks down. A man who was only a man and said the things Jesus said wouldn't be a great moral teacher. If a teacher tells you he can forgive your sins, will judge the world, and existed before Abraham, and it isn't true, he isn't wise and he isn't humble. He's either deceiving you, which destroys his moral authority, or he's sincerely deluded about who he is on a scale that undermines everything else he says, including the ethics you wanted to keep. Lewis put the choice starkly: liar, lunatic, or Lord. The one option the documents don't leave open is the popular one, the fine human teacher who never claimed anything more.

A thoughtful skeptic has a fourth option, and I want to name it rather than pretend the argument is airtight. He may say the claims are legend: Jesus never said these things, and the church put them in his mouth later. That's a serious objection, and feeling its force isn't a sign of weak faith. It moves the question onto history, onto whether the sources are early and reliable, which is where the next session goes. But notice what the legend theory admits even as it objects. The Jesus who reaches us in the actual documents isn't a mild teacher. He's a man making staggering claims. The only way to keep him mild is to decide in advance that the documents are wrong.

And we have to include ourselves here, because most of us prefer the admired Jesus to the real one. Admiration is safe. You can admire someone from a great distance without moving an inch. What we don't want is what he actually asks, which no mere teacher has the right to ask. Socrates asks you to think. Jesus asks for everything, your allegiance and your very self, and he rests the demand not on the brilliance of his arguments but on who he is. He presses it on each person directly: "But who do you say that I am?" (Matthew 16:15). The question this session leaves isn't whether Jesus was admirable. Almost everyone grants that. It's who he thought he was, and what you'll do with the answer.

scriptureStudy.note: "Who can forgive sins but God alone?" The scribes grasp the claim exactly. Jesus isn't moralizing. He's exercising a prerogative that belongs to God.
"Before Abraham was, I am." Jesus uses the name God gave Moses, and his hearers pick up stones, because they hear it as a claim to deity.
"I and the Father are one." When he asks why they want to stone him, they say, "because you, being a man, make yourself God" (John 10:33).
"He was teaching them as one who had authority, and not as their scribes." Even his manner was a claim: "You have heard that it was said... But I say to you."
"I am the way, and the truth, and the life. No one comes to the Father except through me." He doesn't point past himself to the truth. He makes himself the way.
"Are you the Christ, the Son of the Blessed?" And Jesus said, "I am." Under oath and facing death, he affirms the claim.
"But who do you say that I am?" Jesus won't let the question stay at the level of other people's opinions.

sessions.goingDeeper:
The idea that the divine Jesus is a later invention has a long scholarly history, and a group should know its shape rather than fear it. Successive "quests for the historical Jesus," from the eighteenth century through the Jesus Seminar in the late twentieth, tried to strip away supposed legend and recover a merely human teacher. The questions they raise about sources and dates are real questions.

Weigh them against the serious replies. N. T. Wright has written at length on Jesus in his Jewish setting. Richard Bauckham, in Jesus and the Eyewitnesses (2006), argues that the Gospels rest on eyewitness testimony. And many scholars date the creed Paul quotes in 1 Corinthians 15 to within a few years of the events. Note too that Lewis's argument was never meant as a complete proof. It clears away the comfortable middle option so the real question can be asked: did the central thing the documents report actually happen?
sessions.caseStudy:
Suppose a woman in your group has been a comfortable churchgoer for twenty years. She loves the gentle Jesus who blessed children and said, "Let him who is without sin among you be the first to throw a stone." After reading Mark straight through, she comes back unsettled. "I've been reading around the hard parts my whole life," she says. "I knew the kind sayings by heart, and somehow I never noticed him forgiving sins or accepting worship or saying he'd judge the world."

What troubles her isn't that the claims are there. It's that she'd built a faith that avoided them. Sit with what she's discovered: a faith can be sincere and long-held and still rest on a Jesus assembled to our liking. Ask your room gently which sayings of Jesus they know by heart, which ones they've been reading around, and what would change if they let the whole figure speak.
