sessions.title: The Tomb
sessions.aim: To put the central claim of the faith where it belongs, on the table as a historical question, refusing both the believer who treats the resurrection as a feeling and the skeptic who waves it away without weighing the evidence.
sessions.summary:
Christianity isn't a philosophy that happens to have a founder. It's a claim about an event: a man publicly executed was, three days later, alive again, and many people said they saw him. Paul stakes everything on it: "If Christ has not been raised, then our preaching is in vain and your faith is in vain" (1 Corinthians 15:14).

The skeptic's strongest point is that dead people don't rise, so any natural explanation should be preferred. That's a fair starting point. But each natural explanation has to account for stubborn facts: the claim of an empty tomb in the city where he was buried, appearances to groups and to former skeptics, and witnesses who suffered rather than take back what they said they'd seen. The resurrection isn't offered as a leap in the dark. It's offered as the best explanation of those facts, the kind of conclusion a historian or a jury reaches.

keyScripture.why: "And if Christ has not been raised, then our preaching is in vain and your faith is in vain" (1 Corinthians 15:14). Paul doesn't protect the faith from the question. He stakes it on an event that could, in principle, be shown false, and tells the skeptic exactly where to aim.

discussion.q: Read 1 Corinthians 15:12-19. What does it tell you that Paul stakes the whole faith on a single event that could in principle be disproven?
discussion.behind: Most people expect religion to protect itself from disproof. Here the apostle hands the skeptic the lever. Let the room feel that this is the move of someone claiming something happened.

discussion.q: Dead people don't rise. Why might that very fact be a reason to examine the claim rather than dismiss it?
discussion.behind: The skeptic is right that resurrection is wildly improbable on its face, and the believer should grant it. The early witnesses needed extraordinary reasons to believe it, and their behavior needs explaining. Help the room weigh, not assume.

discussion.q: Walk through the natural explanations together, that the body was stolen, that the witnesses hallucinated, that they went to the wrong tomb, that Jesus only fainted. Which seems most plausible to you, and what does it have to explain?
discussion.behind: Let the room think like jurors rather than receive a conclusion. Take each theory seriously and ask what it must account for, especially a tomb the authorities could have checked and the reports of group appearances.

discussion.q: People die for things they believe are true. Why might it matter that the first witnesses claimed to have seen Jesus themselves?
discussion.behind: Many people suffer for sincere beliefs they received from others. The apostles claimed to be eyewitnesses. For them, the choice under pressure was between what they knew they'd seen and a story they'd have known was invented. Don't overclaim it as proof.

discussion.q: Where does the resurrection feel most real to you, and where does it feel hardest to believe?
discussion.behind: Model that doubt is often faith's companion, not its enemy. Invite people to name both the pull and the resistance without resolving them. Go first.

objections.objection: Dead people don't come back to life. A miracle is by definition the most improbable event, so any natural explanation, even an unlikely one, is more reasonable. The evidence would have to be impossible.
objections.response: The premise is right. Dead people don't rise, which is exactly why the disciples themselves didn't expect it and first dismissed the women's report as "an idle tale" (Luke 24:11). But see what "prefer any natural explanation" costs once you apply it. You have to commit to a specific explanation and defend it, and each one strains against a particular fact. A stolen body has to explain why the authorities, who wanted the movement dead, never produced the corpse; Matthew even reports that the counter-story they spread assumed the tomb was empty (Matthew 28:11-15). Hallucination has to explain reports of appearances to groups, including people who hadn't believed. The swoon theory has to explain how a flogged and crucified man convinced his followers he'd conquered death. The skeptic doesn't get to rest in "it must have been something natural." He has to name the something and watch it strain. The claim is only that the resurrection explains the facts better.

objections.objection: People die for false beliefs all the time. The suffering of the apostles proves they were sincere, not that they were right.
objections.response: Sincerity isn't truth, and people have died bravely for false things throughout history. But there's a distinction. Most martyrs die for a belief they received from someone else. The apostles weren't in that position. They claimed to be the eyewitnesses: we saw him, we ate with him after. Acts records them beaten and jailed for saying so (Acts 5:40-41), and James the brother of John put to death (Acts 12:2), and early Christian tradition holds that Peter and Paul died in Rome. For them the choice wasn't between dying and denying something they sincerely believed. It was between holding to what they said they'd seen and abandoning a story they'd have known they made up. People suffer for convictions they hold. It's much harder to explain people suffering for a lie they themselves invented, when a word would end it. That doesn't prove the resurrection like a theorem, but it makes "they simply made it up" hard to sustain.

sessions.quietRoomQuestion: If you became persuaded that the tomb was empty and the man was alive, what is the first thing in your life you suspect you wouldn't want to change?
sessions.practice: This week, think like a juror rather than a spectator. Take the natural explanation for the empty tomb you find most plausible, and spend twenty minutes trying to make it account for all the facts: the empty tomb, the appearances, the witnesses who wouldn't recant. Write down where it holds and where it strains. Then sit for a moment with the possibility that the explanation Christians have always given is the simplest one.
sessions.closingPrayer: Lord, if you were raised, then everything is different, and if you weren't, we're spending an evening on a beautiful mistake, and Paul says so himself. We don't want a faith built on pretending. We want to know what happened. For those of us who believe, steady us when the doubt comes back at night. For those of us who can't yet believe, give us patience to weigh this fairly rather than dismiss it out of habit. If the tomb was empty because you walked out of it, make us willing to deal with a living person and not just an old story. Amen.
reflection: Have I examined the evidence for the resurrection, or only assumed a conclusion in one direction or the other?
Which natural explanation do I lean on, and have I tested whether it accounts for the facts?
Is my resistance really about the evidence, or about what believing would cost?
sessions.teaching:
At its root, Christianity isn't a philosophy of life with a charismatic founder attached. Strip everything else away and what's left is a claim about an event. A man named Jesus was publicly arrested, tried, flogged, and executed by Roman soldiers who knew their work. He was buried. Three days later his tomb was found empty, and over the following weeks many people, in groups and alone, said they'd seen him alive, eaten with him, and touched him. That's the claim. Not that his teaching lived on, or that his spirit was somehow still with them, but that the dead man was bodily alive.

What should stop the skeptic and the believer alike is that the faith doesn't hide this behind a wall of mystery. Paul puts it on the table and hands the skeptic the knife. "And if Christ has not been raised, then our preaching is in vain and your faith is in vain" (1 Corinthians 15:14). "If in Christ we have hope in this life only, we are of all people most to be pitied" (1 Corinthians 15:19). That isn't how someone writes who is protecting a belief from scrutiny. He's staking everything on one event and telling you where to aim if you want to bring it all down.

He also tells you what he received and passed on: "that Christ died for our sins in accordance with the Scriptures, that he was buried, that he was raised on the third day in accordance with the Scriptures, and that he appeared to Cephas, then to the twelve. Then he appeared to more than five hundred brothers at one time, most of whom are still alive" (1 Corinthians 15:3-6). Many scholars think this creed goes back to within a few years of the events. And "most of whom are still alive" is an invitation: go and ask them.

The skeptic's objection deserves its full strength. Dead people don't rise. That isn't a prejudice; it's one of the most reliable observations in human experience. A miracle is by definition an improbable event, so, the skeptic reasons, any natural explanation should be preferred. I grant all of that. Dead men don't rise, which is why nobody was expecting this, why the disciples first heard the women's report as "an idle tale, and they did not believe them" (Luke 24:11), and why Thomas said, "Unless I see in his hands the mark of the nails... I will never believe" (John 20:25). The improbability isn't something the believer should hide from. It's the reason the event is worth examining instead of assuming in either direction.

But see what happens when you stop saying "it must have been something natural" in the abstract and name the something. Take the stolen body. If the authorities wanted to stop a movement preaching resurrection in the same city a few weeks later, the simplest answer was to produce the body. Matthew reports that the story they spread instead was that "his disciples came by night and stole him away" (Matthew 28:13), a story that itself assumes the tomb was empty. If the disciples took it, we're left with men suffering for something they knew was a fraud. Take hallucination. Grief can produce vivid experiences, but the reports describe groups, and they include people who hadn't believed: James the brother of Jesus, and Paul, who had been persecuting the church. Take the swoon theory, that Jesus fainted and revived. It asks us to believe that a man scourged and crucified, sealed in a tomb without food or care, recovered on his own and then appeared to his followers in such a state that they hailed him as the conqueror of death rather than rushing him to a physician. Each theory can be stated. None carries the weight without strain.

Then there's the behavior of the witnesses. People die for false beliefs, so suffering alone proves sincerity, not truth. That's correct as far as it goes. But the apostles weren't ordinary martyrs dying for a report they'd received. They claimed to be the eyewitnesses. Acts tells us they were beaten and ordered to stop, and "they left the presence of the council, rejoicing that they were counted worthy to suffer dishonor for the name" (Acts 5:41). James the brother of John was killed with the sword (Acts 12:2), and early Christian tradition holds that Peter and Paul died in Rome. For them the choice under pressure was between what they said they'd seen with their own eyes and a story they'd have known they invented. People suffer for convictions they hold. It's very hard to explain people suffering for a lie they themselves made up.

None of this proves the resurrection the way two and two make four. History doesn't offer that kind of proof, and neither does a courtroom. But it makes the resurrection the best explanation of a body of evidence the alternatives strain to cover, the conclusion a fair juror might draw, not a feeling a believer works up. And no one should stand over this as if it were easy. Doubt visits believers on certain gray mornings. I'm not asking you to feel a certainty no one feels every day. I'm asking you to stop treating the resurrection as a mood to summon or dismiss and start treating it as a claim to weigh, the most consequential claim ever made, offered as the best account of why that tomb was empty and why frightened men became people who would rather suffer than say it never happened.

scriptureStudy.note: "Christ died for our sins in accordance with the Scriptures... he was buried... he was raised on the third day." Material Paul received and passed on, which many scholars date to within a few years of the events.
"He appeared to more than five hundred brothers at one time, most of whom are still alive." Paul names living witnesses, in effect inviting readers to go and ask.
"If Christ has not been raised, then our preaching is in vain and your faith is in vain." Paul stakes the faith on an event and refuses to protect it from the test.
"These words seemed to them an idle tale, and they did not believe them." The disciples' first reaction was disbelief, which undercuts the idea that they were primed to imagine a resurrection.
Thomas won't believe on report alone. The Gospel keeps the doubter in the story, treating a demand for evidence as something that can be answered.
The guards are paid to say the disciples stole the body. Even the counter-story assumes the tomb was empty.
"This has not been done in a corner." Paul tells a Roman official the events were public and could be looked into.

sessions.goingDeeper:
This is where Christianity invites investigation rather than retreat. Some scholars, such as Gary Habermas, have built the case on facts that most historians who study the period accept, believers and skeptics alike: that Jesus died by crucifixion, that his followers had experiences they took to be appearances of the risen Jesus, that they were transformed from frightened deserters into bold preachers, and that former skeptics such as James and Paul came to believe. Many, though not all, also accept that the tomb was found empty. The debate is mostly about which explanation best fits these facts.

Read the strongest skeptical accounts, such as Bart Ehrman's, which grant the disciples' experiences while explaining them as visions. Weigh them against N. T. Wright's The Resurrection of the Son of God (2003), which argues that neither Jewish nor pagan ideas of the time can account for the specific shape of the early Christian claim, and Frank Morison's Who Moved the Stone? (1930), which by his own account began as an attempt to disprove the resurrection. The discipline is to refuse both the credulity that never examines the alternatives and the skepticism that rules out the supernatural before looking. Ask the historian's question: which explanation accounts for all the facts with the least strain?
sessions.caseStudy:
Suppose an attorney in your group says, half joking, that he could pick apart the resurrection the way he picks apart weak testimony in court. You ask him to try, out loud, taking the case for the prosecution. He chooses the stolen-body theory and builds it carefully. Then, being fair, he stops. "The problem is, I can't explain why the authorities, who wanted this dead, never produced the body. In a real trial that ends it."

Then he says what matters most: "I think I've spent years assuming a natural explanation without ever making myself name one and test it." Ask your room to do what he did: not wave at the case against the resurrection, but build it and test whether it carries the weight. Or have they held a verdict they never put on trial?

memoryVerse.text: Christ died for our sins in accordance with the Scriptures, that he was buried, that he was raised on the third day in accordance with the Scriptures.

sessions.title: Faith and the Honest Doubt
sessions.aim: To recover what faith is, the reasonable trust of a person who has weighed the evidence, and to refuse both the believer who treats doubt as sin and the skeptic who treats faith as believing what you know isn't true.
sessions.summary:
The word "faith" has been damaged from two directions. Many skeptics hear it as believing without evidence, even against it. Many believers hear doubt as faith's opposite, a failure to hide. Neither is what the Bible means.

There's a kind of religion that is blind and anti-intellectual, and it has done real harm. But biblical faith is trust placed in a person on the basis of what you've come to know about them, the same kind of trust you place in a surgeon or a spouse: never total certainty, always enough warrant to act. And doubt isn't faith's opposite. Unbelief is, the settled refusal to trust. Doubt is the wrestling of someone still in the relationship. The father who cried, "I believe; help my unbelief!" (Mark 9:24) wasn't turned away. His son was healed. A faith that has never been questioned isn't strong, only untested.

keyScripture.why: "Immediately the father of the child cried out and said, 'I believe; help my unbelief!'" (Mark 9:24). He holds faith and doubt in the same breath, and Jesus doesn't rebuke the mixture. He heals the boy.

discussion.q: When you hear the word "faith," what does it mean to you? Believing without evidence, trusting a person, hoping against the odds, or something you've never quite defined?
discussion.behind: Almost everyone, including many believers, has absorbed the skeptic's version. Bring the working definition into the open before offering the biblical one.

discussion.q: If faith is trust in a person based on what you've come to know of them, like trusting a surgeon or a spouse, does that change how you see it? Where does it still feel like a stretch?
discussion.behind: Let people name where trust outruns the evidence, because all trust does a little. That's normal, not something to paper over.

discussion.q: Read Mark 9:14-29. What does the father bring to Jesus, and what does Jesus do with it?
discussion.behind: The father's faith is mixed and trembling, and Jesus meets it. Many people believe they must resolve all doubt before they can come. Let the room feel the mercy here. Keep it tender.

discussion.q: What's the difference between doubt and unbelief? How does that land on your own experience of doubting?
discussion.behind: This is the hinge. Many people carry secret doubts they think disqualify them. Help them hear that wrestling is a way of holding on, not letting go.

discussion.q: Where has avoiding your hardest questions weakened your faith rather than protected it?
discussion.behind: Many of us protect our faith by refusing to ask the hard thing and call it loyalty. Buried doubts don't die; they fester. Go first, naming a real question you've had to face.

objections.objection: Faith is just believing things without evidence, or against it. If you had good reasons, you'd call it knowledge. The word itself admits you're believing what can't be shown.
objections.response: That kind of faith exists, and it's worth attacking. There's a blind religion that treats questions as betrayal, and it has earned the skeptic's contempt. But it isn't what the Bible means. The New Testament word for faith is the ordinary word for trust, and it's never defined as belief without grounds. It's trust placed in a person on the basis of what you've come to know about them. You let a surgeon operate on you, not with certainty and not blindly, but because of her training, her record, and what others say about her. You trust a pilot, a spouse, a friend the same way. All of life runs on that kind of trust. Faith in God isn't an irrational exception. It's trust in a person, grounded in evidence, aimed at the one the evidence has been pointing to.

objections.objection: If I have real doubts, then I don't really have faith, and I should either fake it or stop pretending. A true believer wouldn't lie awake wondering whether any of it is true.
objections.response: This needs a gentle answer, because it's the voice of someone who thinks their honesty has locked them out. The opposite of faith isn't doubt. It's unbelief, the settled refusal to trust, the closed door. Doubt is different. It's the wrestling of someone still in the relationship, still coming back to argue with God, which is itself a way of holding on. The Psalms are full of it: "How long, O LORD? Will you forget me forever?" (Psalm 13:1). The father who brought his son to Jesus prayed, "I believe; help my unbelief!" (Mark 9:24), and Jesus didn't send him away to sort out his theology first. He healed the boy. Scripture even commands, "Have mercy on those who doubt" (Jude 22). The faith worth having isn't the absence of questions. It's trust that has walked through the questions and is still holding on.

sessions.quietRoomQuestion: What's the doubt you've never said out loud in church, the question you suspect would get you a worried look instead of an answer?
sessions.practice: This week, do the opposite of what shame tells you to do with your doubts. Write down the hardest question you carry about the faith, in plain words, without softening it. Don't try to answer it yet. Then bring it to God out loud, the way the father did. Tell him the doubt directly. Notice whether saying it to him, rather than hiding it from him, changes how it feels to carry.
sessions.closingPrayer: Lord, we've been taught to hide our doubts from you as if you didn't already know them. Forgive the church for shaming the questioners, and forgive us for faking a certainty we didn't have. We bring you what the father brought, belief and unbelief together, and we ask you to do with it what you did with him: not to reject the mixture but to meet it. Where our faith is real, strengthen it. Where it's doubt, help our unbelief. We're still here, still asking, and we trust that the asking is a kind of holding on. Amen.
reflection: Which definition of faith have I been carrying, and how does the difference change what's being asked of me?
Have I confused doubt with unbelief?
What hard question have I been avoiding, and is the avoidance making my faith stronger or only untested?
sessions.teaching:
The word "faith" has been damaged from both directions, and before we ask anyone to have it, we need to rescue it. From the skeptic's side, faith has come to mean believing without evidence, or against it, switching off the mind in favor of comforting fictions. Mark Twain, in Following the Equator, has a schoolboy say that faith is "believing what you know ain't so," and much modern contempt for religion takes that as the real meaning of the word.

The believer has to admit something uncomfortable here. There is a religion that fits the caricature. There's a blind, anti-intellectual piety that treats every question as an attack and every doubt as sin, and it has driven thoughtful people out the door convinced that to believe they'd have to stop thinking. Grant the skeptic his target. That faith deserves to die. But it isn't the faith of the Bible. The New Testament word translated "faith" is the ordinary Greek word for trust, the word you'd use for relying on a friend, and it's never defined as belief without grounds. It's trust placed in a person on the basis of what you've come to know about that person.

Think about how trust works in the rest of your life. You lie on a table and let a surgeon you met last week cut into you, because of her credentials, her record, and the testimony of others she has operated on. You board a plane and trust your life to a pilot you'll never see. You marry someone and promise them your future on the basis of years of knowing them, and still without certainty, because no amount of knowing closes the gap entirely. Every relationship that matters runs on trust that's warranted but not proven, a commitment that goes one step past the evidence. That's what faith in God is. Not a strange and irrational kind of belief reserved for the gullible, but trust in a person, grounded in what the evidence has been pointing to. Hebrews puts it this way: "Now faith is the assurance of things hoped for, the conviction of things not seen" (Hebrews 11:1). Assurance and conviction aren't the words of wishful thinking.

Now the other damage, the kind that lives inside the church: the assumption that doubt is faith's opposite. Many sincere Christians carry their doubts like a secret shame. They lie awake wondering whether any of it is true and conclude that the wondering proves they don't really believe. That conclusion is false, and it does enormous harm. The opposite of faith isn't doubt. It's unbelief, a settled posture, a closed door, the decision to stop dealing with God altogether. Doubt is the opposite of a closed door. It's the wrestling of someone still inside the relationship, coming back at three in the morning to argue with a God he isn't sure is there, and that coming back is itself a way of holding on.

Jacob wrestled all night and said, "I will not let you go unless you bless me," and was given a new name: "for you have striven with God and with men, and have prevailed" (Genesis 32:26, 28). The Psalms are full of people shouting their doubts at heaven: "How long, O LORD? Will you forget me forever? How long will you hide your face from me?" (Psalm 13:1). Those prayers weren't edited out for being faithless. They were kept as Scripture. Even James's warning against the one who doubts, who is "like a wave of the sea that is driven and tossed by the wind" (James 1:6), is aimed at the "double-minded" (James 1:8), the person who won't commit, not at the person bringing honest questions.

The clearest word is the father in Mark 9. His son has been tormented since childhood, the disciples couldn't help, and he says to Jesus, "If you can do anything, have compassion on us and help us." Jesus answers, "'If you can'! All things are possible for one who believes." And the father cries out, "I believe; help my unbelief!" (Mark 9:22-24). He holds faith and doubt in one breath, and Jesus doesn't tell him to come back when the doubt is gone. He heals the boy. He answers the mixed, trembling faith of a desperate father, because that's the faith real people have.

Many of us think the strongest faith is the one that has never been questioned, and that's backward. A faith that has never been tested isn't strong. It's untested, like a bridge that has never carried a load. You don't know what it will bear until the weight comes. The faith that holds when the diagnosis comes or the grave opens isn't the faith that never doubted. It's the faith that walked through the doubt, asked the worst question out loud, and came out still holding on, not because every question got answered, but because somewhere in the wrestling it found that the One it was wrestling had never let go.

scriptureStudy.note: "I believe; help my unbelief!" The father confesses faith and doubt together, and Jesus heals his son anyway.
"Now faith is the assurance of things hoped for, the conviction of things not seen." Assurance and conviction, not blind wishing. Trust in what is real though not yet seen.
Jesus invites Thomas to touch the wounds rather than scolding him for needing evidence, then blesses "those who have not seen and yet have believed."
"How long, O LORD? Will you forget me forever?" The psalmist brings his doubt straight to God, and the prayer is kept as Scripture.
"Have mercy on those who doubt." Scripture's own instruction about doubters is mercy.
Jacob wrestles until daybreak and won't let go, and is given a new name. The wrestling isn't punished. It marks him.

"The one who doubts is like a wave of the sea that is driven and tossed by the wind." Read with verse 8, James is warning against double-mindedness, the refusal to commit, not against honest questions.

sessions.goingDeeper:
The idea that faith and reason are enemies is contradicted by the church's own history. Augustine urged believers to believe in order to understand, and Anselm in the eleventh century made "faith seeking understanding" a motto. Thomas Aquinas built his method on stating the strongest objections to a position before answering them, which is exactly the habit the caricature says faith forbids. The same tradition also held that faith is finally a gift and a trust, not the conclusion of an argument: reason can bring you to the threshold, and crossing it involves the whole person.

In the twentieth century C. S. Lewis reasoned his way out of atheism and, in Surprised by Joy, described himself as perhaps the most reluctant convert in all England. Timothy Keller, in The Reason for God (2008), argued that believer and skeptic alike live by commitments that can't be finally proven, so the question isn't whether you have faith but which faith holds up best under examination. A group might weigh the claim that doubt brought to God, rather than hidden from him, is one of the ordinary ways faith grows from something inherited into something owned.
sessions.caseStudy:
Suppose a man in your group has been a believer for thirty years. He has served, given, and led, and he has never told anyone that for most of those years he has quietly wondered whether any of it is real. He's been sure the doubt would disqualify him, so he hid it, and the hiding exhausted him. When the group reaches the father in Mark 9, he finally says it out loud. The room doesn't flinch. A younger member says quietly that he'd assumed this man was the one person there who never struggled.

Notice the cost here: not the doubt itself, but the secrecy around it. Ask your room what they've never said out loud in church because they were sure it would get a worried look instead of a welcome, and what the hiding has cost them.

memoryVerse.text: Now faith is the assurance of things hoped for, the conviction of things not seen.

sessions.title: The Call to Follow
sessions.aim: To bring the study to the invitation underneath all the evidence and argument: Christianity is finally not a set of propositions to agree with but a person to follow, and to count fairly both what that costs and what it gives.
sessions.summary:
Everything so far has been clearing the ground. None of it is the point. The point is a person who met fishermen at their nets and didn't hand them a worldview to evaluate. He said, "Follow me" (Mark 1:17). You can believe a fact at a distance and never move. He won't settle for that.

The seeker's fair suspicion is that this is the catch: the reasonable evidence was the setup for an unreasonable demand. There is a cost, and Jesus never hid it. He told people to count it. But the seeker who fears losing his life hasn't heard the other half: "Whoever loses his life for my sake and the gospel's will save it" (Mark 8:35). Everyone already serves something, and most of those masters are harsher than Christ. The study doesn't end in a tidy decision. It ends with a person, asking the question the evidence was always leading to: not "Do you find this plausible?" but "Will you follow me?"

keyScripture.why: "And Jesus said to them, 'Follow me, and I will make you become fishers of men.' And immediately they left their nets and followed him" (Mark 1:17-18). He doesn't ask them to evaluate a doctrine. He calls them to himself.

discussion.q: Five sessions have been about evidence and argument, but Jesus met the fishermen with two words. Why does it matter that the faith ends in a call to follow rather than a conclusion to accept?
discussion.behind: Gather the whole study. The reasoning was real and necessary, but it always pointed past itself to a person. Move the room from evaluating Christianity to reckoning with the one it's about.

discussion.q: What's the difference between believing things about Jesus and following him?
discussion.behind: Many people sincerely believe the facts and have never moved an inch. Help the room see that faith isn't finished when the mind is convinced.

discussion.q: Read Luke 14:25-33. Why do you think Jesus was so open about the cost instead of offering an easier version?
discussion.behind: Jesus often made it harder to follow him, not easier. A faith that hides the cost is selling something he never sold, and his openness about the price is part of what makes the offer trustworthy.

discussion.q: Jesus says whoever loses his life for his sake will find it. Where have you seen, even in small ways, that holding your life tightly is the way to lose it?
discussion.behind: The promise sounds like word play until you test it. Grasping at control, approval, and security tends to hollow life out; giving it away tends to fill it. Look for concrete examples.

discussion.q: Looking back over all five sessions, where do you stand tonight? Is what stands between you and following a question of evidence, a question of cost, or fear?
discussion.behind: Close with invitation, not pressure. Don't force a decision. Invite each person, the leader first, to name where they are. An evidence problem and a cost problem are answered differently.

objections.objection: So this is the catch. All the reasonable evidence and the fair treatment of doubt was the windup, and now comes the pitch. Give up your whole life and follow. The reasonableness was bait for an unreasonable surrender.
objections.response: The suspicion is fair, and I won't soften the cost, because Jesus never did. Following him is total, not a hobby added to an unchanged life. He said to count the cost before you build, said following him could cost family, comfort, even life, and watched crowds walk away rather than change the terms. So something total is being asked. But look at what that surrender is. Every person already serves something: money, approval, appetite, the opinion of others, the endless project of the self. Those are harder masters than Christ, and most of us never chose them; we drifted into their service. The call to follow isn't trading freedom for slavery. It's trading masters you didn't choose for a Lord who says, "I am gentle and lowly in heart" (Matthew 11:29), and who gave his life for you first.

objections.objection: I'm not good enough to follow Jesus. If following means becoming the kind of person he describes, I'm disqualified before I start.
objections.response: This misunderstands the gospel in a way that's freeing to correct. Following Jesus isn't first a moral achievement you produce to qualify. It's a response to grace you don't qualify for. When Peter first saw who Jesus was, he said, "Depart from me, for I am a sinful man, O Lord" (Luke 5:8), and Jesus called him anyway. Peter later denied him three times, and Jesus restored him. The point of the cross is that he came for people who aren't good enough, and there's no other kind of person. You don't clean yourself up to follow him. You follow, and the change happens slowly, over a lifetime, by his power. The call isn't to the qualified. It's to the willing, and the willingness can be as small and as mixed as "I believe; help my unbelief."

sessions.quietRoomQuestion: If Jesus stood in front of you tonight, the real one and not the tame one, and said "Follow me," what's the one thing you're most afraid he'd ask you to leave at the nets?
sessions.practice: This week, before deciding anything, take twenty minutes alone and write two lists side by side. On one, write what following Jesus would actually cost you, specific things named plainly. On the other, write what you're currently serving instead, the things you organize your life around now, and what they've actually given you. Don't rush to a conclusion. Let the two lists sit next to each other, and ask which master you'd rather have.
sessions.closingPrayer: Jesus, you didn't hand the fishermen a worldview to grade. You said, "Follow me," and they left their nets. We've spent these weeks weighing and questioning, which was right, but it was always leading here, to you, asking. We won't pretend we aren't afraid of the cost; you never asked us to pretend. But we're beginning to see that we already serve harder masters than you, and that the life we're clutching is slipping away anyway. Give those who are ready the courage to follow, and give those who aren't the honesty to keep looking. We come with the little faith we have and the doubt that comes with it, and we ask you to make it enough. Amen.
reflection: Have I treated Christianity as a set of claims to evaluate and never reckoned with a person saying "Follow me" to me?
Is my real obstacle a question about whether it's true, or a clear sense of what it would cost?
What am I serving instead of Christ, and what has it given me?
sessions.teaching:
We've spent five sessions clearing the ground, and the clearing was necessary. We asked whether there's a God and found that the world points without forcing. We asked who Jesus thought he was and found a man who left us no room to call him merely a teacher. We asked whether anything happened at the tomb and found evidence the natural theories strain to cover. We asked what faith and doubt are and found that faith is warranted trust and doubt isn't its enemy. All of it was worth doing, and none of it was the point.

Christianity, in the end, isn't a worldview you adopt after the arguments come out in its favor. It's a person. When he walked along the Sea of Galilee and came upon fishermen at their nets, he didn't sit down and offer them a case to evaluate. "Jesus said to them, 'Follow me, and I will make you become fishers of men.' And immediately they left their nets and followed him" (Mark 1:17-18).

Why does he ask for following and not just believing? Because you can believe a fact and never move. You can be persuaded that there's a God, that Jesus is who he claimed, that the tomb was empty, and hold all of it at arm's length like a verdict in a case that doesn't concern you. Jesus won't accept that, because he isn't asking to be agreed with. He's asking to be followed. It's the difference between believing a doctor's diagnosis and taking the medicine, between admiring a road and walking down it.

The seeker's hesitation deserves to be heard at its strongest, because it's fair, and many people in the room feel it even if they haven't said it. So this is the catch. All that reasonable evidence, all that fair treatment of doubt, was the windup, and here's the pitch: give up your whole life. I won't insult you by denying the cost, because Jesus never denied it. "For which of you, desiring to build a tower, does not first sit down and count the cost, whether he has enough to complete it?" (Luke 14:28). He said following him could divide a family. He said, "If anyone would come after me, let him deny himself and take up his cross and follow me" (Mark 8:34), and to his hearers a cross meant a brutal public execution, not a piece of jewelry. When many disciples turned back, he didn't soften the terms. He asked the twelve, "Do you want to go away as well?" (John 6:67). So the suspicion is right that something total is being asked.

But the seeker has heard only half, and the other half changes everything. You aren't free now. Every human being is already following something, already serving some master that organizes the life and demands the sacrifices: money for some, the approval of others for some, appetite for some, the exhausting project of building and defending the self for many. These are real masters, harder than Christ, and most of us never chose them. We drifted into their service. So the call to follow Jesus isn't the loss of a freedom you currently have. It's the chance to trade masters you didn't choose for a Lord who says, "Take my yoke upon you, and learn from me, for I am gentle and lowly in heart, and you will find rest for your souls" (Matthew 11:29), and who showed what he thinks of you by dying for you first.

Then comes the promise that sounds like a riddle and turns out to be one of the truest things ever said about being human. "For whoever would save his life will lose it, but whoever loses his life for my sake and the gospel's will save it" (Mark 8:35). Test it against your own experience. The person who clutches hardest at security and control and approval finds life going dead in his hands. The person who lets go, who gives his life to God and to others, somehow finds it fuller than the grasping ever made it. Jesus isn't asking you to throw your life away. He's telling you the only way to find it, and offering himself as the one worth losing it for. When the crowds left and Jesus asked if the twelve would leave too, Peter answered, "Lord, to whom shall we go? You have the words of eternal life" (John 6:68). That isn't naive. It's the answer of someone who has looked at the alternatives.

So this study doesn't end in a tidy decision you can check off and file away. It comes to rest with a person standing in front of you. No one who follows him will pretend the following is always easy or that doubts never return. But the witness of the church over two thousand years is that this is the best trade a person can make, and that the one who asks for everything is the only master who first gave everything. "Behold, I stand at the door and knock. If anyone hears my voice and opens the door, I will come in to him and eat with him, and he with me" (Revelation 3:20). He knocks. He doesn't break the door down. The evidence was always leading here, not to a conclusion you agree with, but to a question he asks, the same one he asked at the nets: will you follow me?

scriptureStudy.note: "Follow me, and I will make you become fishers of men." Jesus calls people to himself before he explains anything. The heart of the faith is allegiance, not only agreement.
"Which of you, desiring to build a tower, does not first sit down and count the cost?" Jesus tells people to weigh the price before following, the opposite of hiding the fine print.
"Let him deny himself and take up his cross and follow me. For whoever would save his life will lose it." The cost is named plainly and joined to the promise.
"Take my yoke upon you, and learn from me, for I am gentle and lowly in heart." The Lord who asks for everything is a gentle master.
"Lord, to whom shall we go? You have the words of eternal life." Following isn't naive. It's the choice of someone who has weighed the alternatives.
"Depart from me, for I am a sinful man, O Lord." Peter feels unworthy, and Jesus calls him anyway. The call is to the willing, not the qualified.
"Behold, I stand at the door and knock." Christ's posture is a knock, an invitation that waits for an answer.

sessions.goingDeeper:
In much of modern Christianity the call to follow has been reduced to a single decision cut off from a whole life. Dietrich Bonhoeffer, the German pastor executed by the Nazis in April 1945, named this in The Cost of Discipleship (1937). Cheap grace, he wrote, is grace without discipleship, forgiveness preached without repentance. Costly grace is the treasure hidden in a field for which a man sells everything (Matthew 13:44): costly because it cost God his Son, and costly because it calls a person to follow. The English translation carries his best-known line: "When Christ calls a man, he bids him come and die."

Read that against the opposite danger, the legalism that turns following into moral effort to earn what was always a gift, and ask how the tradition held grace and cost together. Weigh, too, the long literature of conversion: Augustine's Confessions, the story of a restless, resisting man finally giving way, and C. S. Lewis's account in Surprised by Joy of being brought in, as he put it, kicking and struggling. Following has rarely been a smooth emotional yes. More often it's a long, argued, resisted reckoning with a person who won't leave you alone.
sessions.caseStudy:
Suppose a young professional tells the group in the last session that she believes all of it now, God, the claims, the tomb, and still hasn't followed. She wants to know why she's stuck when the case is closed in her mind. You ask carefully: is what's holding you back another piece of evidence, or a cost? She goes quiet, then names it. There's a relationship, a way of living, and a sense of being in charge of her own life that she knows following would change. She's been telling herself she needs more proof when she already has enough and is afraid of the price.

Once she can say it's a cost and not a question, the conversation becomes real. Help the group see the difference: an evidence problem and a cost problem are answered in completely different ways, and we often disguise the second as the first because a question feels more respectable than a fear. Ask your room which one is really holding them.

memoryVerse.text: If anyone would come after me, let him deny himself and take up his cross and follow me. For whoever would save his life will lose it, but whoever loses his life for my sake and the gospel's will save it.

leaderPrimer:
Assume nothing when this group sits down. That's the discipline the study asks of its leader, and it's harder than it sounds, because church people run on assumed knowledge the way a town runs on plumbing, invisibly and constantly. Someone at your table doesn't know what the word "gospel" means. Someone else thinks faith means making yourself believe something you suspect is false, and has quietly concluded they can't do it. If you speak insider language, these people won't stop you. They'll nod, go home, and not come back, and you'll never know which sentence lost them.

The hazard is speed. Every session covers ground a lifelong Christian crosses without noticing: the existence of God, the identity of Jesus, the empty tomb. A new believer or a seeker is crossing it for the first time with everything they have. Set your pace by the slowest honest question in the room, not by the material. Let people say half-formed things without correcting them into silence. Treat the question that sounds elementary as what it often is, the bravest sentence spoken that night. Say out loud that no question is too hard to ask here, and when you don't know an answer, say so.

The study is built for the outsider: evidence before invitation, ground cleared before anyone is asked to build on it. Honor that order. The final session is a call to follow, and you'll feel the pull to hurry toward it, to get someone across the line while the room is warm. Resist it completely. A decision pressured into being in week five won't survive week six. A person given room to weigh the claims is being treated the way God treats them, and they can feel the difference even if they can't name it. Keep the room slow, the words plain, and the claims of Jesus at the center. Nothing that happens at the beginning of a faith is small.

faq.q: Is this study going to pressure me to convert before I'm ready?
faq.a: No, and it works to prevent exactly that. It's built for weighing, not for closing a sale, and the leader is asked not to rush anyone toward a decision. The final session ends with a question left open: will you follow me? You're invited to weigh, to question, to take longer than the group would like, and to come freely or not at all. Your freedom to decide, including to say "not yet," is respected.

faq.q: Do I have to already believe to do this study?
faq.a: Not at all. It's written for new believers, for seekers, and for groups with both in the room. The seeker who has decided nothing isn't a project to complete. The new believer who has said yes but doesn't yet know what they said yes to will find the reasons underneath it. You need only be willing to ask real questions and weigh the answers.

faq.q: Does Christianity actually have evidence, or is it blind faith?
faq.a: The study argues that it has evidence. Session one treats the existence of God as a real question where the evidence points without forcing. Session two looks at what Jesus actually claimed in the earliest sources. Session three treats the resurrection as a historical question, weighing the empty tomb, the appearances, and the behavior of the witnesses. Session four shows that biblical faith was never meant to be belief without evidence but trust in a person. The study doesn't claim mathematical proof, which no large question about meaning ever yields. It claims the faith is reasonable, the kind of verdict a fair juror could reach.

faq.q: What if I have serious doubts? Can I still be part of this?
faq.a: Yes, and your doubts are welcome. Session four argues that doubt isn't the opposite of faith. Unbelief is, the settled refusal to trust. Doubt is the wrestling of someone still in the relationship. The father in Mark 9 said, "I believe; help my unbelief!" and Jesus healed his son. A faith that has never been questioned isn't strong, only untested.

faq.q: Isn't Jesus just a good moral teacher? Why do I have to think he was God?
faq.a: Because the Jesus of the earliest documents made claims that don't fit that category. He forgave sins, accepted worship, said "before Abraham was, I am," and said what people do with him decides their eternity. C. S. Lewis argued that a man who says such things can't be merely a wise teacher: either the claims are true, or he was lying, or he was deeply deluded. Session two also takes up the objection that the claims were added later, and points it toward the historical evidence.

faq.q: How can anyone believe a dead man came back to life?
faq.a: Session three grants the skeptic's strongest point first: dead people don't rise, and a miracle is by definition improbable. Then it asks the skeptic to name a specific natural explanation and test it. A stolen body has to explain why the authorities never produced the corpse. Hallucination has to explain group appearances. The swoon theory has to explain a crucified man convincing people he'd conquered death. The study doesn't claim proof beyond all doubt. It claims the resurrection is the best explanation of the evidence.

faq.q: If the witnesses suffered for their belief, doesn't that just prove they were sincere?
faq.a: The study makes that distinction. Sincerity isn't truth, and people have died for false things. But the apostles weren't passing on a report they'd received. They claimed to be the eyewitnesses. For them the choice was between what they said they'd seen and a story they'd have known they invented. People suffer for convictions they hold; it's much harder to explain suffering for a lie you made up yourself. That doesn't prove the resurrection like a theorem, but it makes "they invented it" hard to sustain.

faq.q: What does it actually cost to follow Jesus?
faq.a: The study doesn't hide the cost, because Jesus didn't. He told people to count it and said following him could divide families and lead to a cross. But session five also presses the other half. Everyone already serves some master, money, approval, appetite, the project of the self, and these are harder masters than Christ. The call to follow is a trade of masters you didn't choose for a Lord who is gentle and gave his life for you, with the promise that whoever loses his life for his sake will find it.

faq.q: I'm not good enough to follow Jesus. Does that disqualify me?
faq.a: No. Following Jesus isn't a moral achievement you produce to qualify. It's a response to grace you don't qualify for. Peter said, "Depart from me, for I am a sinful man," and Jesus called him anyway; Peter later denied him three times and was restored. You don't clean yourself up to follow him. You follow, and the change comes slowly, by his power. The call is to the willing.

faq.q: I'm a skeptic. Is this just a sales pitch dressed up as openness?
faq.a: It's a fair suspicion, and the study tries to earn your trust. It grants the skeptic's strongest points: the world doesn't prove God like a theorem, some belief is a crutch, dead people don't rise, and there's a blind religion worth attacking. It states objections at their strongest before answering, and where it doesn't have a clean answer, the leader is asked to say so. It doesn't promise following will be easy, and it ends with the decision open. You're asked to weigh the case and follow it wherever it leads.

faq.q: How do I lead this if I still have doubts of my own?
faq.a: Your doubts aren't a disqualification. The study is built to be led by someone who has found enough to stake a life on but hasn't stopped asking. Every question comes with a note and every session ends in prayer, so you aren't improvising the case. Naming your own hardest question may be the most helpful thing in the room. What you do need is to love people rather than defeat them, keep the room safe for the unsure, say "I don't know" when you don't, and point everyone, yourself first, to the Christ who says "Follow me."

facilitatorScript.open: Welcome, and thanks for being here. Questions of belief are some of the hardest things to talk about in a room. Three things before we start. First, this is a safe room. You can say, "I'm not sure I believe any of this," and raise the hardest objection you have, and nobody will pounce on it or fire a verse at it to make it go away. Second, this study respects your mind. It isn't here to corner anyone. It states the hard objections at their strongest, and where the answers are hard, it says so. No question is too hard to ask here. Third, I'm in this with you. I don't think doubt is foreign to faith, and I won't pretend otherwise. Tonight we're looking at ________. Let me read our passage, and we'll sit with it a moment before anyone speaks.
facilitatorScript.transition: We've looked at what the passage says and weighed it as carefully as we can. Now let's bring it into the week ahead, into the ordinary Tuesday and the three in the morning when the questions come back, because that's where this matters or doesn't.
facilitatorScript.close: We'll stop here, even though it isn't all settled. Faith doesn't arrive on a schedule, and pretending otherwise would be dishonest. Sit with tonight's questions this week rather than burying them. Try the practice, and spend some time with the reflection questions on your own. If you're still carrying a hard question, good. Bring it back next time, out loud, because the asking is part of how this works. Let me pray for us before we go.

cadences.name: The full study (8 weeks)
plan: Week 1: Orientation. Read the summary together, agree that this is a safe room for doubt, and say plainly that no question is too hard to ask.
Week 2: Session 1, Is There Anyone There.
Week 3: Session 2, Who Did Jesus Think He Was.
Week 4: Session 3, The Tomb, part one: the resurrection as a historical question.
Week 5: Session 3 continued: weighing the natural explanations one by one, as jurors.
Week 6: Session 4, Faith and the Honest Doubt.
Week 7: Session 5, The Call to Follow.
Week 8: Look back over the five sessions and where each person stands now, with room for anyone ready to take a next step or keep asking.

cadences.name: The intensive (4 weeks)
plan: Week 1: Sessions 1 and 2 together: the question of God and the claims of Jesus.
Week 2: Session 3, The Tomb, with extra time on weighing the natural explanations.
Week 3: Session 4, Faith and the Honest Doubt.
Week 4: Session 5, The Call to Follow, with a short closing conversation.

cadences.name: As written (5 weeks)
plan: Week 1: Session 1, Is There Anyone There.
Week 2: Session 2, Who Did Jesus Think He Was.
Week 4: Session 4, Faith and the Honest Doubt.
Week 5: Session 5, The Call to Follow.

bibliography.title: Mere Christianity
bibliography.author: C. S. Lewis
bibliography.note: The classic case for the reasonableness of the faith, including the argument at the center of session 2, from a man who came out of atheism.

bibliography.title: The Reason for God: Belief in an Age of Skepticism
bibliography.author: Timothy Keller
bibliography.note: States the strongest objections to Christianity before answering them (2008). Useful across all five sessions.

bibliography.title: Making Sense of God: An Invitation to the Skeptical
bibliography.author: Timothy Keller
bibliography.note: Argues that secularism rests on commitments of its own (2016). Session 1.

bibliography.title: The Resurrection of the Son of God
bibliography.author: N. T. Wright
bibliography.note: A major scholarly study of the early Christian resurrection claim in its Jewish and pagan setting (2003). Session 3.

bibliography.title: Jesus and the Eyewitnesses: The Gospels as Eyewitness Testimony
bibliography.author: Richard Bauckham
bibliography.note: Argues that the Gospels rest on eyewitness testimony (2006). Session 2.

bibliography.title: Who Moved the Stone?
bibliography.author: Frank Morison
bibliography.note: A journalist's examination of the evidence around the empty tomb, which by his own account began as an attempt to disprove it (1930). Session 3.

bibliography.title: The Case for Christ
bibliography.author: Lee Strobel
bibliography.note: A journalist and former skeptic interviews scholars about the historical evidence for Jesus (1998). Sessions 2 and 3.

bibliography.title: The Case for Faith
bibliography.author: Lee Strobel
bibliography.note: Takes up hard objections, including suffering and doubt, in interview form (2000). Session 4.

bibliography.title: The Cost of Discipleship
bibliography.author: Dietrich Bonhoeffer
bibliography.note: The source of the distinction between cheap grace and costly grace (1937). Session 5.

bibliography.title: Confessions
bibliography.author: Augustine of Hippo
bibliography.note: The story of a restless, resisting man surrendering to God. Sessions 1 and 5.

bibliography.title: Orthodoxy
bibliography.author: G. K. Chesterton
bibliography.note: A lively defense of the faith as the explanation that best fits the strange facts of human experience (1908). Sessions 1 and 4.

bibliography.title: Gentle and Lowly: The Heart of Christ for Sinners and Sufferers
bibliography.author: Dane Ortlund
bibliography.note: On Jesus' description of his own heart in Matthew 11:29 (2020). Session 5.

furtherReading: Mere Christianity, C. S. Lewis, for the foundational case for the reasonableness of the faith.
The Reason for God, Timothy Keller, for the strongest objections stated and answered.
Who Moved the Stone?, Frank Morison, for weighing the evidence around the empty tomb.
The Cost of Discipleship, Dietrich Bonhoeffer, for counting the cost session 5 names.
Confessions, Augustine of Hippo, for one man's long, resisted surrender to the God he couldn't outrun.

glossary.definition: The good news at the center of the faith, that God became man in Jesus, lived the life we couldn't, died the death we deserved, and rose again, so that whoever turns and trusts him is forgiven and made new. News about what God has done, not advice about how to be good.
Not belief without evidence but trust placed in a person on the basis of what you've come to know about them, aimed at the God the evidence points toward.
The wrestling of someone still in the relationship with God, still asking. A way of holding on, which Scripture meets with mercy.
The settled refusal to trust, the closed door. The true opposite of faith.
The claim that Jesus, after a public execution and burial, was bodily alive again three days later and seen by many. Paul says the faith stands or falls on it.
C. S. Lewis's argument that a man who claimed what Jesus claimed can't be merely a good teacher, but must be a liar, a lunatic, or the Lord he said he was.
God's ongoing care for and governance of the world he made.
God's unearned favor toward people who don't qualify for it, received with an empty hand.
Bonhoeffer's name for grace cut off from discipleship, forgiveness preached without repentance.
The whole life of following Jesus, not a single decision filed away.
The turning of the whole person away from self-rule and toward God. Not only feeling sorry but changing course.
The reasoned defense of the faith, giving real answers to real objections. Here it serves love, clearing obstacles so a person can see, not defeating an opponent.
An approach to the resurrection that starts from the facts about Jesus' death and its aftermath that most historians of the period accept, and asks which explanation fits them best.
